prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: After reading the full set of opening ballots I am moving optical lattice clocks to the top of my list, ahead of my own first choice. Six of eight members ranked B025 and every one of them proposed the same two names, which is rare. As an instrument builder I judge it on the criteria I care about: a clean idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler and recoil shifts), a decisive experimental realisation (Ye's group taking Sr clocks to the 10^-18 level), and independent confirmation, since many national laboratories now reproduce the accuracy and run clock-to-clock comparisons that agree far below the old caesium standard. The consequences are concrete and lasting: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, and the basis for a redefinition of the second. The two-name attribution has little contest among us. A single-achievement, two-laureate prize is a tidy configuration that I would expect the committee to be able to agree on.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier recognition of precision metrology: the 2005 frequency-comb prize (Hall, Hansch) that Ye's clocks depend on, and the 2012 prize (Wineland) for single-ion control. A sceptic will call this a refinement of recognised tools and a metrology or technology result rather than a discovery. Attribution is also not airtight: Takamoto and Lemonde (and other groups for the early Sr/Yb demonstrations) can be argued for, and I cannot settle that from the ballots. Finally, I am an astroparticle experimentalist, so on atomic-physics priority questions I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson more than on my own judgement.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the kind of new measurement capability where precision limits knowledge, with a clean two-laureate configuration, and the 2005 comb prize leaves room for the clock itself.
responses.response: I agree on the criterion and I now rank B025 first on it. I would add a calibration-minded point: the strength of the case is that the 10^-18 figure is not one laboratory's claim but is reproduced and cross-compared between institutions. That is what separates a believed result from a record. I do not fully share your view that the comb prize leaves plenty of room. Ye's work leans on the comb, so the citation should name the lattice clock itself and its accuracy, not generic precision spectroscopy.

responses.point: The magic-wavelength lattice clock with Ye's 10^-18 demonstration is precise physics where atomic structure theory meets experiment, but overlap with Hall-Hansch and Wineland, and whether Ye's thorium nuclear clock belongs in the citation, are open.
responses.response: Your caveat about the thorium work is the right one and I would keep it out of the citation. The nuclear clock is not yet a mature, independently confirmed result of the same standing, and folding it in would weaken a clean case. On overlap I part ways with you slightly: Hall-Hansch and Wineland honoured the enabling tools, whereas the lattice clock is a distinct device concept with its own validation. I would still want you to tell us whether the atomic-structure side, for example the blackbody and lattice-light-shift evaluation, is robust enough to support the stated uncertainties.

responses.point: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect are a lasting new class of quantum matter, with Kane-Mele theory and Molenkamp's HgTe measurement forming a natural theory-experiment triad, and his first choice.
responses.response: I take this seriously and I keep B036 as my first alternative. I disagree with calling it timely without qualification. You and Mehlig both note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan sit outside the trio, and with the 2016 topology prize in the background that omission is the sharper vulnerability. A prize that leaves out the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested would be contested. Can you say whether the committee can defend the trio as it stands, since I defer to you on condensed matter?

responses.point: IceCube's diffuse flux, TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic-plane signal opened neutrino astronomy, but he ranks it only fourth because source identification is still developing and the prize may be early.
responses.response: We reached the same view independently, and I will be frank that it moves me. I ranked IceCube first at the opening stage, but only two of us ranked it. Your point about unidentified sources is fair: the diffuse flux is firm, while the source population is still thin. I am not dropping the case, because the instrument is a major achievement, but I keep it as an alternative rather than the lead. I disagree somewhat with the worry about Baikal credit. That affects the name list, not whether the discovery stands.

responses.point: Circuit QED is a regime-opening platform, strongly confirmed over two decades, that follows the 2025 prize without duplicating it, though he flags possible bias as a close colleague of the community.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure. My reservation is the one Kroll raises: with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits so recent, a second superconducting-circuit prize this year looks too close. I also see the credit split (Blais or Girvin as third) as unresolved even by your account. I did not rank B016 at opening and I do not now, but I would want to hear whether you consider it distinct enough from the 2025 work to stand without strain.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Lemonde or others have a credit claim on the early lattice-clock demonstrations that would change the two names.
Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as a metrology or technology result rather than physics discovery, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D topological insulator credit problem can be resolved well enough to prefer B036.
Whether IceCube source identification will be firm enough for a later prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B025: my work is PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, none of which involves lattice clocks or the named laureates. For B007 I work in the same broad astroparticle field and the Fermi-LAT collaboration contributed to the TXS 0506+056 multimessenger follow-up, so I have noted this, but I have no personal or institutional tie to IceCube, Halzen or Spiering.
